newsitem.title: USA: Nearly 99,000 possibly exposed to Gulf War gas -US.
newsitem.headline: Nearly 99,000 possibly exposed to Gulf War gas -US.

text.p: Nearly 99,000 U.S. troops may have been exposed to low levels of Iraqi nerve gas in the 1991 Gulf War, the Defence Department said on Thursday, adding that long-term medical effects were unlikely.

But two experts with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) acknowledged that data on human reaction to small amounts of the chemical was sparse, and they did not rule out possible health consequences.

The new figure was five times the Pentagon's earlier estimate for the number of U.S. personnel exposed to nerve gas, and was based on a Central Intelligence Agency model aimed at seeing the path of a plume of vaporised sarin gas that rose from an Iraqi weapons depot at Khamisiyah.

Starting on March 10, 1991, when the depot was blown up, the plume of gas may have drifted nearly 300 miles (480 km) south and west of the weapons dump before dissipating four days later, said Bernard Rostker, the Pentagon's special assistant for what has come to be called Gulf War illness.

The number of U.S. personnel who may have been exposed to low levels of the nerve agents sarin and cyclosarin is now estimated at 98,910, and the Defence Department was notifying those people by letter beginning on Thursday.

"When rockets were destroyed in the pit area of Khamisiyah on March 10, 1991, the nerve agents sarin and cyclosarin may have been released into the air," the letter to affected veterans read. "If you were with your unit at this time, you may have been in an area where exposure to a very low level of nerve agents was possible."
The veterans were asked to contact special registries at the Defence Department and VA if health concerns persisted.

Rostker said at a briefing that researchers knew of no U.S. military unit that got a high enough dose of nerve gas to produce its first effects, which include tightness in the chest, wheezing and runny eyes.
Of 7,400 veterans who were within about 30 miles (50 km) of Khamisiyah who responded to a Pentagon inquiry about nerve gas effects, only 26 reported such symptoms, Rostker said.
Rostker said health studies of those who may have been exposed to the gas would continue, as would investigations of otherwise unexplained ailments suffered by Gulf War veterans.

Asked repeatedly whether it was premature to say, as the Pentagon did in a statement, that "current medical evidence indicates that long-term health problems are unlikely," Dr. Thomas Garthwaite, the VA's undersecretary for health, said, "In the absense of data, can you say one thing or another?"
Dr. Susan Mather, a VA expert on environmental hazards, acknowledged in response to a question that it may be too early to say what the danger level of exposure is.

"As we understand it today, we know of no risks that this (low-level exposure to nerve gas) would incur," Mather said. She noted that there is data on animals for high-level exposure, but said "we don't have a lot of knowledge of human beings on that low level."

Asked to comment on how Thursday's announcement fit into the inquiry into illnesses related to the Gulf War, Rostker responded: "I think we're much closer to solving the mystery because for the first time, we have an exposure with an assessment of what the dosage was, what the effect was."
Representative Chris Shays, a Connecticut Republican who chairs a House of Representatives panel dealing with Gulf War ailments, expressed outrage at the new numbers.

"... As late as May 1996 the Pentagon was denying that U.S. troops were exposed to chemical weapons," Shays said in a statement. "Since then the numbers of exposed troops have risen from zero to nearly 100,000. We suspect that these numbers will continue to rise as other exposures in other locations are finally revealed."
Defence Department estimates late last year had said about 20,000 U.S. troops had been within 30 miles (50 km) of Khamisiyah and could thus have been exposed.
